evidence_quotes.quote: Using observations and in-depth interviews with small-scale sanitation service providers, this study investigated the constraints and motivations of sanitation-related businesses in peri-urban communities in the Ningo–Prampram district of Ghana.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5 of 7 (Constraints to sanitation business)
evidence_quotes.quote: previously, there were three dumping sites for fecal sludge but all have been sold to individuals for their private businesses, a situation which compels us to travel long distances at higher costs to dump fecal sludge

Using the three SSPs (masons, pit-emptier, hardware suppliers) as case studies, an empirical investigation was made into the internal and external factors that constrain and/or motivate sanitation business in the study area.

Notwithstanding the threat of the constraints, it was found that the small-scale sanitation service providers are making a healthy proﬁt margin, which serves to motivate them to stay and continue in their respective businesses.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although motivated by low sanitation coverage in peri-urban Ghana, the study does not examine household or community sanitation service access; instead, its unit of analysis and focus are the entrepreneurial constraints and financial viability of six small-scale private sanitation businesses (three latrine masons, two hardware suppliers, and one pit-emptier).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No. The study does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements for connection, tariff rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure governing user access); instead, it ranks general small-enterprise operational constraints (primarily delayed client payments, irregular cash flow, hardware costs/quality, and lack of bank credit). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2: Borderline/incidental at best — the paper briefly notes institutional and administrative challenges facing small businesses (Registrar General business registration costs/bureaucracy, registration needed for District Assembly contracts, privatization/sale of three fecal sludge dumping sites, tax burdens, land litigation, and unauthorized police stops), but even if Criterion 2 were treated as satisfied under its plain broad wording, the overall decision remains exclude because the study measures enterprise constraint rankings and business profit margins rather than household or community sanitation service access outcomes (failing Criteria 1 and 4).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data from a descriptive and explanatory multiple-case study of six small-scale sanitation service providers using transect walks and structured/semi-structured interviews conducted in 2012-2013.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The reported outcomes are provider-side rankings of small-business constraints (Table 2) and business operating revenues, costs, and profit margins (27-46%, Table 3) motivating entrepreneurs to remain in business. Household or community sanitation access, coverage, connection, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes are not measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. For its own research question, the study clearly identifies the study population and unit of analysis (six small-scale sanitation businesses in four peri-urban communities of Ningo-Prampram district), business constraint factors, enterprise profitability/constraint outcomes, and multiple-case study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods descriptive and explanatory multiple-case study (transect walk observations and structured/semi-structured in-depth interviews with constraint rankings and profit-margin estimation)
population_and_sample: Small-scale sanitation service providers (SSPs) in four peri-urban communities (Olowey, Kley, Lower East Prampram, and Lower West Prampram) in the Ningo-Prampram district, Greater Accra region, Ghana; purposive/convenience sample of 6 businesses (3 masons/latrine builders, 2 sanitation hardware suppliers, and 1 pit-emptier)
exposure: Internal and external operational constraints on small-scale sanitation businesses (delayed client credit payments, irregular cash flow, hardware quality/prices, lack of bank credit/collateral, sale of fecal sludge dumping sites, business registration bureaucracy/costs, taxation, land litigation, and unauthorized police stops)
outcome: Ranked small-business operational constraints (1 to N ordinal rankings) and enterprise profitability/pecuniary motivation measured via operating profit and profit margins (27% to 46%)
rationale: Exclude (E04 - Wrong outcome; also fails C1 and narrow C2). This mixed-methods multiple-case study interviews six small-scale private sanitation entrepreneurs (three latrine masons, two hardware suppliers, and one pit-emptier) in peri-urban Ningo-Prampram, Ghana, to rank their business constraints and estimate enterprise profit margins (27-46%). It does not examine household or community sanitation service access (C1 = no) and reports no outcome measuring household/community access, connection, service availability, reliability, affordability, or exclusion (C4 = no). It also lacks a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope (C2 = no); even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (noting brief mentions of business registration, tax systems, and privatized dumping sites as small-enterprise constraints), the paper remains excluded because its unit of analysis and outcomes are small-business constraints and profitability rather than sanitation service access.
